content: 주요서비스 바로가기 본문 바로가기 매체정보 바로가기 로그인 바로가기 기사검색 바로가기 전체서비스 바로가기 상단영역 UPDATE : 2026-11-06 19:14 (Fri) Home Log in Join 전체메뉴 뒤로멈춤앞으로 뒤로멈춤앞으로 기사검색 검색 본문영역 뒤로멈춤앞으로 뒤로멈춤앞으로 뒤로멈춤앞으로 뒤로멈춤앞으로 이전 기사보기 다음 기사보기 ‘A Virus Has No Gender’: Korean HPV campaign takes 3rd place at global PR awards 바로가기 복사하기 본문 글씨 줄이기 본문 글씨 키우기 스크롤 이동 상태바 현재위치 Home Pharma ‘A Virus Has No Gender’: Korean HPV campaign takes 3rd place at global PR awards Add KBR as a preferred source on Google 기자명 Kim Yoon-mi Published 2026.11.03 09:12 바로가기 복사하기 본문 글씨 줄이기 본문 글씨 키우기 A virus does not discriminate by gender. That simple message, used to challenge the perception that human papillomavirus (HPV) prevention is primarily a women's issue, has earned a Korean healthcare campaign third place in a global public relations competition. The campaign, “A Virus Has No Gender,” developed by PR Bom and MSD Korea, ranked third at the 2026 Global SABRE Awards held in Chicago last Monday. Organized by PRovoke Media, the competition drew more than 5,500 entries from over 60 countries. The campaign was the only Korean entry among the 40 global winners. The recognition puts a decade-long effort to broaden public understanding of HPV prevention among the top-ranked PR campaigns worldwide. Although HPV is often associated with cervical cancer, the virus can cause diseases in both men and women. MSD Korea and PR Bom built their campaign around that distinction, seeking to shift public perceptions of HPV prevention from a predominantly female concern to a broader public health issue. Their work over the past decade has focused on raising awareness of HPV-related diseases and building public support for prevention policies that address both sexes. From left, PR Bom Manager Kim Su-jin, CEO Jeon Eun-jeong, PRovoke Media Chair Paul Holmes and PR Bom Division Head Kim Ja-young pose at the 2026 Global SABRE Awards in Chicago. (Courtesy of PR Bom) The global ranking follows another award for the same campaign in August, when PR Bom became the first Korean company to receive the Platinum SABRE Award for Best in Show at the Asia-Pacific SABRE Awards in Singapore. At the time, PRovoke Media described the campaign as the culmination of a decade-long effort to influence government HPV vaccination policy. The latest result places the Korean campaign third among the global winners, extending its recognition beyond the Asia-Pacific region. “Ranking third globally after winning the top Asia-Pacific award is meaningful international recognition of the efforts and results we have built with MSD Korea over the past decade,” PR Bom CEO Jeon Eun-jeong said. Jeon said the agency would continue working with clients on disease awareness and public health communications. tweet Related articles PR Bom wins top APAC SABRE award for MSD Korea's gender-neutral Tap to Unmute Key Takeaways Half of women diagnosed with cervical cancer have not been screened within the previous 5 years. Earlier detection is enabling more conservative cervical cancer treatments, including fertility-preserving approaches for some patients. Rates of advanced and metastatic cervical cancer have increased in recent years, driven in part by lack of screening in several populations. At-home HPV testing could help overcome access, cultural, and healthcare engagement barriers that prevent many people from being screened. HPV causes multiple cancers beyond cervical cancer, making gender-neutral vaccination and ongoing screening critical for long-term prevention. Watch part 1 here. This transcript has been edited for clarity. Dr. McDonald: We know about the incidence of cervical cancer, but I want to ask, from the gynecologic oncology perspective, what do you see clinically with patients diagnosed with cervical cancer? How is it different now compared to a few years ago? Dr. Slomovitz: The only thing I really want to add to the screening: I love all the new technology, but you can’t screen if they don’t come to the office. Part of that education is that 50% of women who get cervical cancer have not had a pap within the last five years. So, if patients want to know what’s the first thing they could do—go to their doctor. It’s that simple. The screening tests are all important, but going to the doctor is that first step. Whether it be an at-home test or not, it’s not only the first test that matters. As we know, it’s also important to have appropriate follow-up. Abnormal paps can be cured; HPV can’t be cured. As far as the specific answer to your question, there’s still a bimodal distribution of cases. One is that in those that are getting screening, we’re catching it earlier on. We know this because there’s more of a push towards conservative therapy, when in the past, we couldn’t do that. There’s more of a push towards fertility preservation, not requiring a full hysterectomy, and not requiring a full lymph node dissection. The other distribution of cases that we’re seeing is those that never have screening, those with advanced-stage, widely metastatic disease. Those are the areas where we need to get better. My last comment is that we talk about the numbers in the US, but remember, we’re also a country where a lot of folks come from a lot of different places. I’m from Miami, so we’re a gateway city. You guys could talk about the numbers in the US, but I see a fair number of cervical cancer cases not only from the US, but from South America, Central America, the Bahamas, and the Caribbean area. I think it’s important to understand it’s a global problem, and we see it come back to the US. Thanks. Dr. McDonald: Help us understand, what are some of the challenges when we’re talking about incorporating cervical cancer screening, particularly into primary care visits or barriers to getting people into the office? Dr. Chan: I really appreciate what Dr. Eckhart and Dr. Harper discussed with respects to the advances in technology that allow us to get these patients into screening. As a gynecologic oncologist, unfortunately, over the last 10 years, I’ve been seeing a significant increase in locally advanced and metastatic cervical cancer. In fact, in these last 10 years, the research we’ve done has shown that advanced-stage disease has increased about 2% per year. With the advent of primary HPV screening, this will bring together what Dr. Slomovitz actually just mentioned, which is that 50% of the patients that get diagnosed with these metastatic cancers haven’t been screened over the last five years. By bringing in these patients with at-home HPV testing, I think this will decrease a lot of the barriers that have hindered patients from getting screened or going to the office. In California, we see not just the Hispanic immigrant population, but also the Asian immigrant population. In the research that we’ve done using the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, we found that the Asian subgroups were actually the highest unscreened population, surprisingly, because it’s not just an access to care issue—it’s also a cultural issue. They feel like, “I don’t need to see a doctor unless there’s something wrong.” With the experience of COVID, getting people used to self-testing at home, and even with the genetic screening that’s out there for self-testing, I think HPV self-testing will be much more readily adopted even in patients who are not as health-literate. Dr. McDonald: That’s a great segue to talking more about the gaps and barriers, and then the potential solutions. I know we’ve mentioned this already. Before we move on, we mentioned that this is not just about cervical cancer. HPV causes multiple different types of cancers. Can someone help remind our audience about other types of cancers that can be triggered by HPV infections? Dr. Harper: We know that head and neck cancer is also caused by HPV. We know that it’s more common in men than it is in women. We also know that there’s no screening for head and neck cancer, which is why the numbers of people with head and neck cancer are greater than the numbers of women with cervical cancer. And that is something that we have to deal with in head and neck cancer. But because men are more likely to get head and neck cancer, that makes it even more important that HPV vaccine is a gender-neutral proposition and that we vaccinate both our girls and our boys as early as we can. The FDA approval starts at the age of nine. This is fundamentally important to cancer prevention efforts in many organs, including anal, penile, vaginal, vulvar, as well as head and neck and cervical, which are the primary ones. Dr. Amboree: I would also like to add that a recent study published in JAMA Oncology showed some effectiveness of the HPV vaccine in younger birth cohorts of men, regarding protection against HPV-associated disease. I think that was the first evidence that was published to show those long-term benefits of HPV vaccination specifically in men. So that, again, reemphasizes Dr. Harper’s point that this is important not just for females, but for men as well. Dr. Slomovitz: The one thing that’s super important is the vaginal cancers are sort of a continuum of the cervical issues. People get a hysterectomy for dysplasia for HPV and they’re like, “Okay, I’m done. I don’t need to go anymore.” There are lists of indications why women don’t need paps after hysterectomy. Abnormal HPV for the hysterectomy is not one of them. They still need routine pap smears to prevent vaginal cancer. Particularly in this population of women, they need to get routine screening even after hysterectomy. Dr. Harper: To go off of Dr. Slomovitz, this shows that HPV is a chronic disease. We don’t have a cure for it. Once you’re infected with HPV, you have it. Sometimes it’s not detectable. But once they have an HPV infection, we need to educate our women that this is a chronic disease and that they need to continue their screening through the appropriate age range. Oncology/Hematology > Other Cancers De-Escalated Treatment for HPV-Related Throat Cancer Gets Long-Term Supporting Data — More than 90% of patients alive without evidence of disease at 5 years by Charles Bankhead, Senior Editor, MedPage Today November 3, 2026 • 4 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday Key Takeaways De-escalated treatment for HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer achieved durable cancer control in over 90% of patients. Treatment reduced elective nodal radiation to 30 Gy and omitted low-risk nodal regions without failures. The results add to existing evidence supporting de-escalation for HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer but this particular regimen still requires confirmation in a multicenter phase III trial. Reduced-intensity treatment for human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) led to durable cancer control in more than 90% of patients, long-term follow-up from a prospective study showed. After a median follow-up of 5 years, 94% of patients had no evidence of disease and 90.6% were alive at last follow-up after de-escalated elective nodal irradiation (ENI) during definitive concurrent chemoradiation (CRT). Five-year locoregional control, distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS), and overall survival (OS) exceeded 90%. All but one patient with locoregional failure had recurrences in areas with known residual macroscopic disease. No treatment failures occurred in nodal basins that were omitted from treatment. De-escalation came in the form of 30-Gy ENI instead of the usual 50-60 Gy dose and omission of low-risk nodal basins, reported Nancy Y. Lee, MD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and colleagues in JAMA Oncology. "These outcomes were attained across the spectrum of T- and N-stage groups and smoking histories among patients predominantly treated with concurrent platinum-based chemoradiosensitization," the authors noted. "The systematic omission of uninvolved nodal levels IB/V did not result in failures in those areas and provides a simple class solution to reducing irradiated volume and toxic effects. The 30-Gy ENI dose remains the lowest among published approaches, is tailored to HPV-associated disease, and results in the lowest reported gastrostomy tube insertion rate." "Although low-dose ENI without concurrent chemotherapy has been investigated, recent phase III randomized trials have demonstrated the superiority of concurrent platinum-based chemotherapy for achieving cure in HPV-associated OPC, underscoring the importance of de-escalating ENI within an optimally curative paradigm for HPV-associated OPC," they wrote. The study showed that focusing on radiation dose is not the only strategy to de-escalate treatment for HPV-associated OPC, said David Sher, MD, of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, who was not involved in the study. "While we often focus on the total dose delivered to visible cancer, in actuality, ENI is responsible for a substantial amount of normal tissue irradiation and dose to critical normal structures, such as the salivary glands and swallowing structures," Sher, an expert for the American Society for Radiation Oncology, told MedPage Today. "There has been a progressive recognition that ENI dose can be a significant contributor to quality-of-life outcomes, and there are several studies, both prospective and retrospective, that have shown that the standard dose of 50 Gy can be substantially lowered." "[The] degree of success is remarkable given the extent of dose reduction, and it is exciting to see such superb outcomes," he added. "Although we do not have quality-of-life data from this study, prior reports were also very favorable." Providing additional context for the study results, Sher noted that all patients underwent PET-CT imaging and the vast majority had MRI as well. Such advanced imaging may play a key role in identifying smaller lymph nodes that might harbor cancer and require higher radiation doses. Additionally, all the patients received cisplatin-containing chemotherapy, and HPV-associated OPC is cisplatin sensitive. Also, the authors did not report how many "equivocal" lymph nodes were treated with a higher radiation dose. Results of the current study add to those of a previous phase III trial that used a slightly higher nodal irradiation dose, he added. "All of this work strongly suggests we are delivering ENI doses that are far too high, and we need to be more aggressive in reducing the acute and long-term side-effect burden of our treatments while preserving oncologic efficacy," said Sher. "For such a result to become a true standard of care, though, we do need a phase III randomized study to confirm non-inferiority in a multi-institutional setting, and hopefully such a trial can be available soon to patients and our community." Lee and colleagues previously reported 2-year outcomes with the de-escalation strategy, showing good locoregional control and survival with "excellent" quality of life. The current report aimed to establish the durability of the strategy, as assessed after a median follow-up of 5 years. The analysis involved 276 patients treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy (n=256) or intensity-modulated proton therapy (n=20). Treated nodal and subclinical regions received 30 Gy in 15 fractions and a sequential boost of 40 Gy in 20 fractions. The 5-year results showed that 260 patients had no evidence of disease at 5 years and 250 were alive at last follow-up. Five-year outcomes were: Locoregional control: 97.0% OS: 90.8% Progression-free survival: 85.9% DMFS: 91.2% A single elective nodal failure occurred 6 months after concurrent CRT in a contralateral indeterminate lymph node present at baseline and treated with 30 Gy, the authors reported. The last regional failure occurred 18 months post-treatment. Distant-only recurrences occurred in 23 patients. At last follow-up, 12 of the patients remained alive with no evidence of disease, and one remained alive with disease. Please enable JavaScript to view the comments powered by Disqus

content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 7, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Pocket colposcope triages HPV-positive women with HIV in Kenya trial by November 6, 2026 in Cancer, Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Pocket colposcope triages HPV-positive women with HIV in Kenya trial Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Women living with HIV face a sharply elevated risk of cervical cancer, and the World Health Organization has responded by recommending a “screen, triage, and treat” approach in resource-limited settings, with HPV testing preferred for the initial screen. But a positive HPV test is only the beginning of the decision. Because HPV infection is common and often transient, treating every HPV-positive woman would mean destroying healthy tissue on a large scale, straining clinics and exposing patients to unnecessary procedures. The WHO therefore calls for a triage step before treatment, and in much of sub-Saharan Africa that step is visual inspection with acetic acid, or VIA, in which a provider paints the cervix with vinegar and looks with the naked eye for aceto-white epithelium, the pale patches that can mark precancerous lesions. A new randomized clinical trial from Kisumu, Kenya, tested whether a low-cost handheld device could do that job better. The study, published in the British Journal of Cancer, enrolled HPV-positive women living with HIV across six HIV care clinics in Kisumu between November 2022 and June 2023. Unlike a standard colposcope, which sits outside the patient and demands high-end optics, the Pocket Colposcope is inserted through a speculum and positioned about three centimeters from the cervix, a short working distance that removes the need for expensive magnification systems. It captures white-light and green-light images, and the developers report image quality comparable to standard colposcopes. The device has previously been tested in more than six countries, but this trial was designed to evaluate it as a triage tool specifically among women receiving HIV care in western Kenya, a population with high rates of HPV and precancerous lesions. The design was straightforward and deliberately pragmatic. During routine clinic visits, women living with HIV were offered HPV testing using self-collected cervical samples processed on the Ampfire platform at Lumumba sub-county hospital. Those aged 25 to 65 who tested positive and planned to undergo treatment at the clinic were eligible; pregnant women, women with a history of cervical cancer, and those with suspected infection or invasive cancer were excluded. Of 2,794 women screened, 503, or 18 percent, tested HPV-positive, and 404 of them enrolled and were randomized, stratified by clinic, to either the standard-of-care VIA arm or the Pocket Colposcope arm. A technical error in the randomization scheme left a slight imbalance, with 208 women assigned to VIA and 196 to the Pocket arm. Discover more Engineering job board Research publication platform Scientific instrument sales Laboratory equipment supplier Learn Engineering In both arms, providers applied acetic acid to the cervix and, after sixty seconds, looked for aceto-white epithelium, recording a positive or negative visual diagnosis. Providers in the VIA arm performed the exam unaided, while those in the Pocket arm captured images before and after acetic acid application using both white and green light, though only white-light images were used for diagnosis. Critically, biopsies were taken in both arms either from aceto-white areas or, when none were visible, from two random locations, and every participant’s histopathology served as the diagnostic gold standard. This design matters: many earlier studies of VIA performed biopsies only in women whose visual exam was positive, a verification bias that can inflate sensitivity and make specificity impossible to calculate. HPV-positive women eligible for ablative treatment received it regardless of the visual diagnosis, following WHO recommendations, while women with large lesions or suspected invasive carcinoma were referred for advanced care. The headline numbers showed the two methods performing similarly on most measures. Positive visual exam rates were 17.3 percent in the VIA arm and 14.3 percent in the Pocket arm, a difference that was not statistically significant. The overall rate of CIN2/3, the moderate and severe precancerous lesions confirmed by pathology, was 15.5 percent across the study, split as 12.2 percent in the VIA arm and 18.8 percent in the Pocket arm. Sensitivity for detecting CIN2+ lesions, which included CIN2, CIN3, squamous cell carcinoma, and atypical glandular cells, was nearly identical at 25.0 percent for the Pocket and 26.3 percent for VIA. Specificity was 4.9 percentage points higher in the Pocket arm at 88.9 percent versus 84 percent, while the negative predictive value was 4.2 points lower at 82.9 percent versus 87.1 percent. The most striking difference was the positive predictive value: 37 percent for the Pocket against 20.6 percent for VIA, nearly double, though the authors note this difference was not statistically significant given the number of outcome cases. Discover more Track Biotech Tour Colleges Donate to Research That PPV gap carries real clinical weight. A positive visual exam in the VIA arm was confirmed as disease by pathology only about one time in five, meaning most women flagged for treatment had no precancerous lesion on biopsy. In the Pocket arm, roughly one in three positive exams corresponded to confirmed disease. The trial also found a high rate of CIN3 among the lesions detected, at 17.3 percent of Pocket cases and 9.6 percent of VIA cases, and most biopsies in both arms were histologically negative, at 75.9 percent in the Pocket arm and 80.2 percent in the VIA arm. The distribution of biopsy results did not differ significantly between the arms. The experience data painted an encouraging picture for implementation. Fourteen providers, medical officers and nurses delivering general outpatient and HIV-specific care in government clinics, carried out both exam types based on patient randomization, and most reported no challenges, at 96.0 percent for Pocket exams and 97.1 percent for VIA exams. Fewer than 1 percent reported issues with the device itself, such as internet access, recording patient information, or perceived patient discomfort, and difficulty visualizing the cervix was noted in 2.5 percent of Pocket exams versus 0.5 percent of VIA exams. Providers completed exams and made diagnoses 100 percent of the time in both arms. On the patient side, 190 women in the Pocket arm and 197 in the VIA arm completed surveys. Most participants reported little or no prior knowledge of cervical cancer prevention, but roughly four in five said their knowledge increased after the exam. Nearly all reported little or no pain, expressed confidence in their provider’s assessment, and said they would recommend the exam, with no significant adverse events associated with either device. The trial’s authors are candid about its limits. Despite the overall sample size of 404, the number of CIN2+ cases that formed the outcome was lower than anticipated, which limited the study’s power to detect statistically significant differences in diagnostic accuracy. The randomization imbalance, caused by non-stratified randomization of the last 25 participants, could have introduced bias. Provider turnover and varying levels of expertise with cervical cancer screening methods, encountered because the team deliberately tested the device in a real-world setting, likely contributed to the low sensitivity observed in both arms, and the authors emphasize that methods to standardize training are required when introducing new technologies. Image quality is another concern: blur and glare can obstruct lesions and affect diagnosis, and a companion analysis found that clinical experts’ confidence in identifying lesions was significantly higher for clear images than for blurry ones. The authors plan to incorporate real-time image quality feedback into future deployments and see automated correction algorithms as a path to improving accuracy. Context from the broader literature helps explain why these results matter. Meta-analyses of VIA screening in low- and middle-income countries have reported widely varying sensitivities, from 44 to 83 percent, and specificities from 76 to 91 percent for detecting CIN2+. Studies of VIA specifically as a triage step for HPV-positive women are scarcer, with reported sensitivities ranging from 28 to 82 percent. In this trial, with histopathology on every participant, the specificity of VIA alone, 84 percent, was comparable to prior estimates, while its sensitivity of about 26 percent was on the low end, consistent with a study by Mekuria and colleagues that also biopsied all participants regardless of visual result. The authors also point to the automated visual evaluation algorithm, trained on a database of more than 150,000 cervical images and evaluated across five countries, which showed superior sensitivity to standard VIA with a moderate loss in specificity, as evidence that pairing image-capturing devices with diagnostic algorithms could further improve performance where colposcopy expertise is scarce. The conclusion the authors draw is measured. The Pocket Colposcope was superior at identifying CIN2+ among HPV-positive women living with HIV in western Kenya, they write, though with no significant differences in sensitivity or specificity in this small sample, and the device merits study in larger settings. They position it as an adjunct to VIA that could facilitate biopsy confirmation, support provider training and patient education, and enable remote diagnosis through image transfer, with future work needed on costs and technology requirements before widespread implementation. (IX) participated in the 38th Annual Conference of the International Papillomavirus Society (IPVS 2026), held in Athens, Greece, from October 22 to 25, joining global experts and partners to exchange scientific insights and explore collaborative approaches to HPV prevention and cervical cancer elimination. Under the theme "Together Against HPV," IX welcomed international attendees to Booth 14 for discussions on vaccine innovation, scientific evidence, accessibility and international collaboration. An interactive signature board and message wall invited participants to share their perspectives and commitments to HPV prevention. Recognizing the diverse public health needs and challenges across countries, IX emphasized the importance of listening to global voices, respecting local contexts and translating scientific innovation into accessible, sustainable solutions. IX at IPVS 2026:Listening to Global Voices,Partnering to Advance HPV Prevention New Interim Data Presented at IPVS 2026 During the scientific program, Dr. Nana A. Ansah of Ghana's Navrongo Health Research Centre presented the Month 6 interim analysis of PATH's Single-dose HPV Immunobridging Study with New Vaccines (SHINE I; CVIA 104). This Phase III, double-blind, randomized, multinational study in Ghana and the Philippines compares the immunogenicity and safety of single-dose Cecolin 9 with Gardasil 9 among girls aged 9–14 and young women aged 15–20, respectively. Final data are expected in 2028. Research Findings Presented at IPVS 2026 From Innovation to Global Collaboration IX's HPV vaccine portfolio includes Cecolin, its WHO-prequalified bivalent HPV vaccine, and Cecolin 9, its next-generation 9-valent HPV vaccine launched in China in 2025. Built on its proprietary E. coli-derived virus-like particle (VLP) technology platform, IX continues to advance vaccine innovation, scalable manufacturing and international partnerships. Through technology transfer and local capacity building, IX aims to strengthen sustainable vaccine supply and bring innovation closer to local public health needs. IPVS 2026 reaffirmed IX's commitment to listening, learning and collaborating with the global HPV community. Guided by its mission to provide high-quality, affordable vaccines, IX will continue working with partners worldwide to advance HPV prevention and support the shared goal of cervical cancer elimination. content: 新闻 体育 汽车 房产 旅游 教育 时尚 科技 财经 娱乐 消除宫颈癌,你我共行动 ——“世界消除宫颈癌行动日”科普义诊活动 2026-11-04 16:30 来源: 江南水乡生活见闻 发布于:北京市 宫颈癌居全球女性恶性肿瘤发病数第4位,严重威胁女性健康。但90%以上的宫颈癌与高危型人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)的持续感染直接相关所以宫颈癌是可以预防和治愈的。 2020年11月17日,世界卫生组织(WHO)发布实施《加速消除宫颈癌全球战略》,宣告全球194个国家将在2030年实现“90-70-90”目标: 90%的女孩15岁以前完成人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)疫苗;70%的35~45岁女性接受高质量宫颈癌筛查;90%的确诊宫颈病变女性得到治疗。 中国政府积极响应,2023年1月20日,国家卫生健康委等十部门联合印发《加速消除宫颈癌行动计划(2023-2030年)》,通过促进HPV疫苗接种、加强宫颈癌筛查、规范宫颈癌治疗等三级预防措施有效遏制宫颈癌发病率、死亡率上升趋势,减轻宫颈癌社会疾病负担。 一级预防:促进HPV疫苗接种 90%以上的宫颈癌与高危型人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)持续感染密切相关,其中 HPV16、18 型是最常见的“元凶”,约70%的宫颈癌由其引起。 越早接种HPV疫苗,越早筑起 “防护墙”,是预防宫颈癌最有效的手段。 二级预防:加强宫颈癌筛查 从HPV持续感染,到宫颈发生上皮内瘤变(癌前病变),再进展到宫颈癌,往往需要8-15年的漫长过程。 在这个充足的 “黄金窗口期”,加强宫颈癌筛查,能够及时发现宫颈的癌前病变,及时干预。 推荐21 岁以上有性生活的女性,定期进行宫颈细胞学检查(LCT)和HPV 检测。 三级预防:规范宫颈癌治疗 若诊断发现罹患宫颈癌或癌前病变,也不用担心,及时和规范的治疗是消除宫颈癌的 “最后防线”。 宫颈癌前病变和早期宫颈癌,通过手术根治,治愈率很高; 中晚期宫颈癌,通过放疗、化疗、靶向治疗等综合手段控制病情,延长生存期并改善生活质量。 国妇婴宫颈科建立了多手段精准宫颈癌筛查、精细阴道镜诊断、激光消融/微无创的光动力治疗/LEEP术一站式宫颈癌前病变的治疗及随访体系。同步开设男性HPV筛查与诊疗服务。 国妇婴妇瘤科开展宫颈癌的手术、化疗、靶向和免疫等给予不同期别宫颈癌患者个体化治疗。创新提出宫颈癌的早筛新方法和“坎儿井”微创新术式,相关成果获得上海医学科技奖二等奖。宫颈癌治疗后五年生存率位居上海首位。 “世界消除宫颈癌行动日”当天,宫颈科和妇瘤科将联手为市民带来科普课堂和免费义诊。 返回搜狐,查看更多 阅读 () 平台声明 该文观点仅代表作者本人,搜狐号系信息发布平台,搜狐仅提供信息存储空间服务。

content: SingaporeInternationalChinaBusinessOpinionLifestyleEntertainment Search Hospitals and clinics introduce HPV self-sampling to ease screening discomfort and embarrassment AI-translated article with transliterated names. Read original Chinese article here. Women who opt for HPV self-sampling can insert a soft swab into the vagina to collect a sample in a private space, then submit it for laboratory testing. (Photo: Peter Chew) A growing number of healthcare institutions are offering human papillomavirus (HPV) self-sampling without a speculum, giving women a more private and gentler option for cervical cancer screening. Experts say self-collected samples are as accurate as those taken by doctors, but higher costs and exclusion from Healthier SG remain barriers to wider adoption. Cervical cancer is almost entirely preventable through screening. The World Health Organisation’s targets for eliminating cervical cancer include having at least 90% of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15, and 70% of women screened once by age 35 and again by age 45, by 2030. According to the Ministry of Health’s National Population Health Survey 2025, 47.1% of Singapore residents had undergone cervical cancer screening, slightly higher than 44.9% in 2024. Despite the increase, the rate remains below that of many developed countries. A major barrier is women’s concern about pain, discomfort or embarrassment during conventional screening. Masi, a 32-year-old clinic assistant, experienced severe pain and even bleeding during her first Pap smear at 23. The experience left her deeply distressed, and she did not undergo screening again for several years. “I later started working at a gynaecology clinic, where I was always surrounded by doctors and colleagues who encouraged women to go for screening.” It was only about two years ago, with encouragement from colleagues, that she tried self-sampling and tested positive for HPV. Further tests revealed precancerous changes in her cervix, and she subsequently underwent a cervical cone biopsy. For many women like Masi, the barrier to screening is not necessarily a lack of awareness of its importance, but fear of the pain and psychological discomfort associated with a metal speculum, commonly described in Chinese as “duckbill forceps”. Singapore Cancer Society and SGH introduce HPV self-sampling To ease these concerns, more hospitals and clinics are offering HPV self-sampling. Women can collect a sample themselves with a soft swab in a private space, without a speculum examination, and submit it for laboratory testing. The Singapore Cancer Society began offering self-sampling at SCS Clinic @ Bishan in July this year, becoming the first and only organisation to provide the service at a community clinic. Singapore citizens and permanent residents aged 30 and above can be tested free of charge, regardless of whether they receive Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) subsidies. Last year, the society and the Alliance for Active Action Against HPV (A4HPV) began piloting self-sampling in the community, reaching out to women who rarely undergo screening. The clinic’s senior manager, Renie Liestary, told Lianhe Zaobao (LHZB) that nine of about 200 women tested so far, or 4%, had received positive results. Singapore General Hospital (SGH) spent about two years studying whether HPV self-sampling could reduce women’s reluctance to undergo screening, before introducing it at its gynaecology outpatient clinic in July this year. Dr Yvonne Wong, a consultant at the department of obstetrics & gynaecology at Singapore General Hospital, said the hospital still sees women who have not undergone screening for years and are found to have precancerous cervical changes or even invasive cancer when diagnosed. Dr Wong stressed that self-collected samples are as accurate as those taken by doctors. The hospital has also conducted internal validation, confirming that self-collected samples can be tested reliably using its existing HPV testing platform. Some general practitioner clinics have also begun offering self-sampling. Dr Lai Wern Sheng, medical director of The Good Clinic, which introduced the test this year, said one consideration was that the clinic is staffed by male doctors. It wanted to offer another option for patients who are uncomfortable having an intimate examination performed by a doctor of the opposite sex. However, Dr Lai said fewer than 3% of the clinic’s patients currently opt for self-sampling. The most common concern is the test’s accuracy; healthcare staff are also particularly concerned about the risk of false negatives. Experts: Comparable accuracy, but cost remains a challenge Clinical assistant professor Zhang Zewen, a consultant at the division of medical oncology at the National Cancer Centre Singapore, said data from multiple clinical studies show that self-collected samples have comparable sensitivity to samples taken by doctors in detecting high-risk HPV DNA. “In Singapore, patients generally still prefer to have health checks performed by a doctor. However, self-testing kits are a helpful and accessible alternative for those who are apprehensive of a Pap smear and I would not be surprised to see uptake grow over time as more women become aware of this option.” Zhang said cost remains a barrier to widespread adoption of self-sampling in Singapore. Conventional tests using samples taken by doctors are covered under Healthier SG and receive government subsidies, with citizens paying between a few dollars and $20. Self-sampling generally has to be paid for out of pocket and costs upwards of $100. Dr Ida Ismail-Pratt, a specialist and medical adviser to A4HPV, also sees the exclusion of self-sampling from Healthier SG as one of the main barriers to wider adoption. She hopes that, as public awareness grows, self-sampling will eventually be included in government-subsidised healthcare. DTAP EXPRESS, part of Republic Healthcare, was among the first providers to offer HPV self-sampling at its “doctorless” clinic. As more clinics consider introducing the test, Dr Jonathan Ti Shih Yeung, Group Chief Medical Officer, Republic Healthcare, cautioned that, besides ensuring patients know how to collect samples correctly, providers must also ensure they understand their results and have a clear pathway for follow-up care if they test positive. “Self-sampling is a useful additional option that can complement conventional cervical screening performed by healthcare professionals, rather than necessarily replace it.” This is an AI-translated article and some names may be transliterated. Seegene(31,000 won ▼ 800 -2.52%) said on the 6th that its consolidated operating profit for the third quarter was 11.6 billion won, up 21.2% from the same period a year earlier, based on preliminary figures. Revenue for the same period was 123.1 billion won, up 8.4%. The company said growth in non-respiratory product lines drove results. Sales of human papillomavirus (HPV), sexually transmitted infection (STI), and gastrointestinal (GI) products were 62.4 billion won, up 12.3% from a year earlier. Growth by product line was 19.7% for HPV, 12.6% for GI, and 6.7% for STI. By region in the third quarter, Europe accounted for the largest share of sales at 59.1%, followed by Asia (15.8%), Latin America (13%), Korea (7.3%), and North America (4.8%). Seegene is expanding its direct sales system in Europe, its largest revenue market. The France subsidiary, whose establishment was released in Dec. last year, began direct sales in July this year. It plans to shift the distributor-centered sales structure to a subsidiary-centered one and expand its business into the public tender market and HPV testing. The company said it will develop the France subsidiary, together with the Italy and Germany subsidiaries, into a European business hub.
